Abel Ferro, the tuner, reached the Pellam Street hall on a snowy Thursday, two days before Lise Marrow's recital. Lise, the town's best young pianist, said the old upright had been sounding wrong all winter, flat from top to bottom. Nell Ostrand, the hall's manager, had sent for him, and Edith Garvey, the hall's benefactor, had offered the committee the gift of a new piano if the old one proved worn out.

Owen Dorran, the caretaker, had found the crack the first winter after Tobias Rusk died, and had shown it to Abel. It had opened since the last entry in the notebook where Rusk, Abel's old teacher, logged every tuning, and it was still a hairline split in the board. Nell told Mrs. Garvey of it only this winter, when Lise began to complain. For thirty years Rusk had tuned this piano a shade below standard pitch, and Abel had kept to that pitch at each October tuning since, at the committee's expense. Lise, who practised on the new piano at her school, heard it as flat.

The piano stood where it always had, at the far end from the stove. Abel looked for a broken string, ready to fit a new one, and found every string sound. Lise wanted it at standard pitch for Saturday, though it would pull hard on the split. They struck a bargain: he would bring it up to standard pitch, and she would ring him at the first odd sound.

'Will it be ready for Saturday?' Nell asked. Abel kept his eyes on the split. 'Ready, yes. Keep the stove low and the doors shut till then, and ring me if you hear a crack like a pistol shot. I'll come at six on Saturday to check the board before anyone sits down.' He pencilled his number inside the lid.

On Saturday Lise went through her whole programme at standard pitch without a sour note, and the split held to the last chord. Mrs. Garvey's offer of a new piano stood, in case the board gave way later. Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring bright and true.

passage:
For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and before she had traced a single horse she bought scalpels and a book on stripping old paint. The families who had bought the horses were easy to trace. The first horse she brought home had been stored in the basement of a chapel. After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a school hall, an ivied garden and a hotel lobby in Brannock, until every horse but one was back within the year.

Paying for the restoration was the hard part. The estimate came to forty thousand pounds, the council would give nothing, and a raffle brought in barely a tenth. For four years Nora ran jumble sales and wrote to everyone who had ridden the carousel, and the last of the money arrived a week before the work would have stopped. Everything else went quickly. Tom Avery, an organ builder raised in Callow, rebuilt the band organ's missing front from a photograph taken in 1923; the council agreed in one evening that the carousel should stand on the common again; and the original colours showed plainly under later paint.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. When Nora asked for it, Hal agreed at once. On the drive to the common he asked her twice how high the brook beside it rose in March, and before he let the grey off the trailer he walked to the water's edge, paced the distance back to the platform, and asked where the horses would be stored each winter.

The carousel turned again on the common in July 1996. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

passage:
For sixteen summers Dr. Hana Vell has counted the sand beetles of Orsk Spit, pale hunters the size of a thumbnail. They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

Much had changed on the spit that year. Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence along the south end of the dune foot, beside the car park. A March storm cut into the dune's seaward face, though the crest and the traps came through it. In May a boardwalk opened along the dune, and the park ran its lamps all night, every night. Visitors wore paths across the north hollow, a kilometre past the last trap.

Arkin went first to the notebooks, reading all sixteen in search of an earlier drop that had recovered by itself. He found the 2013 drop, which had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass, and on a page from 2011 a note in Vell's hand: a camper's lamp left on the beach, and beetles heaped around it like spilled rice. That night the two of them walked the boardwalk and found the sand under every lamp crawling with beetles.

Arkin came back to the station at two in the morning with beetles in his hair and down his collar, held out his counter, and asked whether this many still counted as a drop. Vell lifted a beetle off his sleeve, set it on the windowsill, and asked it whether it had paid for its room at the boardwalk hotel.

Vell asked the park to put shades on the boardwalk lamps, so that their glow falls only on the planks. This July the count was six hundred and forty.
